section.title: God's Bounty in Creation
section.sectionRationale: A harvest hymn of thanksgiving that moves from the forgiveness of sins and the privilege of dwelling near God in His temple, through His awesome power stilling the roaring seas and the tumult of the nations, to the overflowing bounty of rain, grain, and pasture across the whole earth, this psalm joins atonement, cosmic power, and harvest praise into a single song.
section.thesis: The God who atones for transgressions and answers awesome deeds of righteousness is the same God who forms the mountains, stills the roaring seas, and crowns the year with such bounty that the very hills and valleys shout for joy, teaching that forgiveness and physical provision both flow from the one God whom all the earth has reason to praise.
section.frameNote: Three movements: praise awaiting God in Zion for atonement and nearness to Him, verses 1-4; His awesome deeds of righteousness stilling seas and nations, hope of the whole earth, verses 5-8; and His overflowing bounty of rain and grain crowning the year, so the pastures and valleys shout and sing, verses 9-13.

units.label: Praise awaits You, O God, in Zion

verses.text: Praise awaits You, O God, in Zion; to You our vows will be fulfilled.
O You who listen to prayer, all people will come to You.
When iniquities prevail against me, You {{kaphar|atone}} for our transgressions.
Blessed is the one You choose and bring near to dwell in Your courts! We are filled with the goodness of Your house, the holiness of Your temple.

units.label: You stilled the roaring of the seas
units.note: awesome deeds of righteousness, the hope of the whole earth

verses.text: With awesome deeds of righteousness You answer us, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas.
You formed the mountains by Your power, having girded Yourself with might.
You stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves, and the tumult of the nations.
Those who live far away fear Your wonders; You make the dawn and sunset shout for joy.

units.label: You crown the year with Your bounty
units.note: overflowing rain, grain, and pasture across the earth

verses.text: You attend to the earth and water it; with abundance You enrich it. The streams of God are full of water, for You prepare our grain by providing for the earth.
You soak its furrows and level its ridges; You soften it with showers and bless its growth.
You crown the year with Your {{tovah|bounty}}, and Your paths overflow with plenty.
The pastures of the wilderness overflow; the hills are robed with joy.
The pastures are clothed with flocks, and the valleys are decked with grain. They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing.

kaphar.gloss: To atone, to cover over, to make propitiation for sin. Named as something only God does for His people's transgressions, this word roots the psalm's praise not merely in creation's bounty but first in the forgiveness that makes nearness to a holy God possible at all.

tovah.gloss: Bounty, goodness, abundant good. God is said to crown the entire year with this quality, an overflowing generosity in the harvest that mirrors, in the physical world, the same goodness of His house named in verse 4.

basic.context: This psalm joins two things that might seem unrelated, the forgiveness of sins and the abundance of harvest. It moves from praise for atonement and nearness to God in His temple, through His power over roaring seas and warring nations, to His overflowing generosity in rain, grain, and pasture across the whole earth.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm teaches that God's spiritual and physical gifts are not separate categories; the same God who atones for sin also waters the earth and gives the harvest, and both call for the same thankful praise.
basic.originalLanguages: God is the one who kaphar, atones, covers over transgressions His people could never manage themselves, verse 3. And He crowns the year with tovah, overflowing bounty, verse 11, an abundant goodness that mirrors, in creation, the goodness of His own house.
basic.typology: The psalm's picture of God stilling the roaring seas and the tumult of nations, verse 7, anticipates Christ, who commands wind and waves directly, Mark 4:39, and whose atonement, foreshadowed in verse 3, is accomplished fully and finally at the cross.
basic.christ: Christ fulfills both movements of this psalm, He is the atonement, kaphar, this psalm names as God's own work, accomplished fully at the cross, Romans 3:25, and He exercises the same divine authority over roaring seas that this psalm attributes to God alone, Mark 4:39, showing Him to be the God this psalm praises in human flesh.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who alone can atone for sin, whose power forms mountains and stills seas and nations, and whose generous hand waters the earth so richly that the created world itself, hills, pastures, and valleys, breaks into shouts of joy and song.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:25 names Christ as the atoning sacrifice, fulfilling this psalm's confession that only God can atone for transgressions. Mark 4:35-41 shows Jesus stilling a literal storm with the same divine authority this psalm ascribes to God over the roaring seas. Matthew 5:45 echoes this psalm's picture of God's provision, sending rain on the just and the unjust alike.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's confession that God alone atones for sin and God alone provides the earth's abundance finds its fulfillment in Christ, whose atoning death answers the psalm's third verse and whose authority over creation answers its seventh, uniting forgiveness and provision in the one Savior.

context.literary:
Psalm 65 is a hymn in three stanzas of four, four and five verses, and each stanza widens the circle. The first is about Zion and the individual: vows, prayer, sins, and a person brought near to live in the courts. The second is about the whole earth and its peoples, where God answers 'with awesome deeds of righteousness,' forms mountains, stills seas and nations, and draws joy from the far east and west. The third is about the soil, the rain and the year, and it finishes with hills, pastures and valleys that shout and sing. A worshipper begins at the altar and ends in a field, and the psalm implies that the two belong in one song.

The stanzas are knit together by repeated words. The 'goodness' of God's house in verse 4 and the 'bounty' with which He crowns the year in verse 11 are the same Hebrew family of words, so the temple's gifts and the harvest's gifts are named alike. Fullness is another thread: the worshipper is 'filled' with the goodness of the house in verse 4, and the streams, the pastures and the valleys are full in verses 9 to 13. The 'You' that opens every major clause is the psalm's grammar of praise. God is the subject of almost every verb, and people and creation are the ones acted upon, so the poem is a long sentence whose subject never changes.

The movement also runs from sin to song. Verse 3 is the dark centre of the first stanza, a confession that iniquities prevail and an answer that God atones. The shift from 'me' to 'our' in that verse is worth noticing, because the individual's guilt is brought into the people's and both are answered together. After that the psalm has no sorrow left in it. Everything from verse 5 on is the speech of people who have been forgiven, for whom the world is now a place to praise in. The psalm has no lament and no request.
context.historical:
Israel's year was bound to the harvest, and so was its worship. The grain harvest in spring and the ingathering of fruit in the autumn were marked by pilgrim feasts at the sanctuary, where people brought firstfruits and vows and rejoiced before the LORD, Deuteronomy 26:1 to 11 and 16:13 to 15. The Feast of Tabernacles followed only days after the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 23:27 and 23:34, and the psalm's pairing of atonement in verse 3 with bounty in verse 11 fits that autumn pattern well. It is one of the reasons the psalm is often linked with the festival season, though the text itself does not name an occasion.

Water was the pressure point of Israel's agriculture. The land depended on the autumn and spring rains and had no great river like Egypt's, so a failed season meant famine. The covenant tied the rains to faithfulness, Deuteronomy 11:14 and 28:12, and Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to hear from heaven and forgive when the skies are shut because of sin, 1 Kings 8:35 to 36. Jeremiah said that Israel had not said in their hearts, 'Let us fear the LORD our God, who gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season,' Jeremiah 5:24. Against that background the psalm's joining of forgiveness and rainfall is not odd. For an Israelite farmer, sin and drought were already connected, so a God who atones is also a God who sends the showers.

The seas in verse 7 and the mention of far-off peoples in verse 8 place Israel within a larger world. Canaan's neighbours told of storm and sea gods who fought for control. Israel's hymn says that the sea and the nations are quieted by the one God, and it makes the point without a battle. The 'farthest seas' and 'the ends of the earth' would have sounded to ancient ears like the edge of the known world, and the psalm places the hope of all of it in the God of Zion.
context.canonical:
The psalm belongs with a group of psalms that join creation and salvation. Psalm 104:13 to 14 also describes God watering the mountains and making the grass grow, and Psalm 147:8 to 9 says that He prepares rain for the earth. Psalm 145:15 to 16 says that the eyes of all look to Him and He gives them their food in season. What sets Psalm 65 apart is that it begins with atonement. The pairing is repeated in Isaiah 55, where an offer of pardon and a picture of rain are set side by side, and the rain that waters the earth is a picture of the word that goes out from His mouth, Isaiah 55:10 to 13. Joel 2:23 to 26 promises restored rains and full threshing floors after the locusts, as part of the repair of a repentant people.

The psalm's universal notes have a long reach. 'All people will come to You,' verse 2, belongs with Psalm 22:27, 'All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD,' Psalm 67:1 to 7, and Isaiah 2:2 to 3, where all nations stream to the mountain of the house of the LORD. Isaiah 56:7 says that God's house 'will be called a house of prayer for all the nations,' and Zechariah 14:16 to 17 pictures the survivors from the nations going up year after year to keep the Feast of Tabernacles.

The New Testament takes up both movements. Paul and Barnabas tell a pagan crowd that God 'has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness,' Acts 14:17, and Jesus says that the Father sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, Matthew 5:45. The atonement of verse 3 is answered in Romans 3:25, 1 John 2:2 and Hebrews 2:17, and the stilled sea of verse 7 is answered in the Gospels when the wind and waves obey Jesus, Matthew 8:26 to 27.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of this psalm wants Israel to hold two things together that we tend to keep in separate rooms. One is what happens at the altar, where vows are paid and sins are dealt with. The other is what happens in the field, where the rain falls and the grain ripens. The psalm teaches the congregation that these are the work of one God, and that the one who deals with the worshipper's guilt is also the one who fills the furrows. A pilgrim singing this on the way to Zion was meant to see the whole year, and the whole world, in the light of his forgiveness.

The psalm also means to fix the order. Forgiveness comes first, in verse 3, and the gifts of the earth follow. It is not that the harvest is a reward for being forgiven, but that the forgiven person is the one who can see the harvest as a gift. The worshipper who has been brought near in verse 4 is the one who can look out and say 'You crown the year.' Ordinary blessings turn into occasions for thanks when the heart has been set right.

Finally, the psalm means to enlarge Israel's vision. The hope of 'all the ends of the earth' and the fear of those who 'live far away' are not afterthoughts. The God of Zion is the God of the seas, the nations and the dawn and sunset. Israel is to praise Him as the people who know Him by name, and to do so in the hearing of a world that has not yet learned to.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a hymn of praise, and most of it describes what God does. It does not say that every harvest will be good or that every drought is punishment. The Bible elsewhere shows faithful people enduring famine, and Habakkuk 3:17 to 18 praises God even when the fields fail. Reading Psalm 65 as a promise of a plentiful year would misuse it. It describes God's general pattern of care, and it teaches Israel to credit the rain to Him, not to a rival power.

What the psalm prescribes is a way of seeing and a practice of worship. Pay vows, and do it in the context of the community. Come to God with the confession that iniquities prevail and trust His atonement. Bring praise to Him in Zion, where the congregation meets. Read the ordinary processes of the world, rain, grain and pasture, as acts of God, and let gratitude follow. The command to take account of the harvest as a gift still applies: Paul teaches that the food God provides is to be received with thanksgiving, 1 Timothy 4:4 to 5, and the psalm is the pattern of that thanksgiving. It also says nothing against the work of farmers and scientists, since the psalm has God preparing the grain through the earth and its furrows.

debates.question: What occasion does the psalm celebrate?

views.label: An autumn harvest thanksgiving, linked to the Feast of Tabernacles
views.case: The ingathering feast followed the Day of Atonement, and the psalm pairs atonement in verse 3 with a crowned year in verse 11. The feast was a time of rejoicing in the harvest, Deuteronomy 16:13 to 15, and later Jewish and Christian use of the psalm has often followed this link. It suits the picture of a people who have been cleansed and now celebrate.

views.label: A thanksgiving after the end of a drought or a national deliverance
views.case: The 'awesome deeds of righteousness' of verse 5 and the stilling of 'the tumult of the nations' in verse 7 suggest a particular rescue, and the rain could be the answer to a prayer like that of 1 Kings 8:35 to 36. On this view the psalm was written after a famine or a war, and the abundance is the sign of restoration.

views.label: A general hymn, used at different times
views.case: The psalm names no date, king or event, and its vows and its praise would suit any of the pilgrim feasts. Its breadth is part of its purpose. It was kept because it could be sung by a people at many points in the year.

debates.bearing: The choice does not change the psalm's teaching that forgiveness and provision come from the same hand. It does change the mood in which one hears it: as a festival song of cleansed people, as the relief after a hard season, or as a standing hymn of a world held together by God.

debates.question: Who are the 'all people' who will come to God in verse 2?

views.label: Israelites from every tribe coming to the sanctuary
views.case: The psalm is set in Zion and begins with vows, so the coming could be the pilgrimage of Israel's families to the temple. 'All flesh' is often used for all living creatures, but in a festival context it can mean every member of the covenant people. On this view the universal language reflects the scope of Israel's own gathering.

views.label: The nations, drawn to the God who hears prayer
views.case: The verse says that all people will come to the One who listens to prayer, and the psalm soon speaks of 'the hope of all the ends of the earth' and of those who live far away fearing His wonders. Elsewhere the prophets describe the nations streaming to Zion, Isaiah 2:2 to 3, and the New Testament takes the line as a promise of the gospel reaching the world.

debates.bearing: The second reading fits the psalm's own growth, since the next two stanzas speak of the nations and the far seas. Whether or not the first hearers understood it so, the psalm opens the door that the New Testament walks through, in which those who were far away are brought near, Ephesians 2:13.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the verb behind 'atone' in verse 3, which is kaphar in its intensive form. God is the subject and sins are the object, and that is how the word is used in the prayers and promises of Psalm 79:9, 'deliver us and atone for our sins,' and Isaiah 6:7, 'your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.' The ritual use is found in Leviticus 16:30, where on the Day of Atonement 'atonement will be made for you to cleanse you.' Although people are the ones who have to bring the offering in the ritual, in this verse God alone carries out the covering. The psalm says also that iniquities 'prevail' against the speaker, a verb that carries the sense of overpowering, which makes the admission honest: sin is stronger than the worshipper, and only God's act is stronger than sin.

The second detail is the pronoun shift in that same verse, from 'me' to 'our,' so the individual speaker becomes a spokesman for the people. The psalm's 'We are filled' in verse 4 continues that plural. Israel prays as a body.

The third is the verb for bringing near. 'Blessed is the one You choose and bring near' uses the verb from which the word for an offering, qorban, comes. The one God brings near has the status of an offering accepted, and he 'dwells' in the courts, with a verb that shares its root with the word for the tabernacle, mishkan. The Hebrew says that God picks the person, draws them close and gives them a dwelling, all in one line, and the verbs belong to the vocabulary of the sanctuary.

The fourth concerns the word for God's 'visit' in verse 9. The verb behind 'attend to' is the one used when God 'visited' Sarah, and in Ruth 1:6 when 'the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food.' It is the verb of gracious notice, not of inspection. The same verse says that God 'prepares' the grain, and a form of the same verb is used in verse 6 of God 'forming' the mountains. One verb covers both the founding of the mountains and the preparation of the grain, so creation and daily provision are a single work of God.

Finally, the verb in verse 11 for 'crown' pictures a wreath placed on the year, and the next clause says that His paths 'overflow,' a word that elsewhere means to drip. The same verb appears in verse 12 of the wilderness pastures. The noun beside that verb, as I read it, is the word for richness that Psalm 63:5 uses of the soul's feast, so the language of abundance crosses from the field to the soul.

typology.type: Atonement and the Day of Atonement, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The psalm says that God covers transgressions. Israel's pattern was the annual ritual of Leviticus 16, when the high priest made atonement with blood, and the feast of harvest followed within days. The escalation in Christ is that He is Himself 'the atoning sacrifice' for our sins and 'not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world,' 1 John 2:2, and the high priest who 'make[s] atonement for the sins of the people,' Hebrews 2:17. The type falls short because the ritual was repeated each year, Exodus 30:10, while Christ's offering is once and for all, Hebrews 9:14.

typology.type: The one chosen and brought near to dwell in God's courts, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: A worshipper who has been cleansed is drawn into the courts and filled with the goodness of the house. The temple was a place of access that only some could enter at certain times. Paul tells the Ephesians that those who were far away 'have been brought near through the blood of Christ,' and that 'through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit,' Ephesians 2:13 and 2:18. Hebrews says that we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, Hebrews 10:19. The type falls short in that the psalm's blessing belongs to a person drawn near to a building, while the New Testament places believers in a living temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

typology.type: The stilling of seas and nations, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: God quiets the roar of the seas and the tumult of peoples. The type is shown in the Gospels when Jesus rebukes the wind and sea and the disciples ask who He is, Mark 4:39 to 41. The psalm says that the power to still the sea belongs to God, as in Psalm 89:9, and the disciples' question answers itself. The escalation is that the stilling happens in the flesh, in a boat, at a word. The type is incomplete at the final stage, since the roar of the nations is stilled only when the Lord brings His kingdom, and Revelation 21:1 says that in the new creation the sea is no more.

typology.type: The watered earth and the crowned year, verses 9 to 13
typology.fulfillment: The land is saturated and overflows with grain and flocks. In Isaiah the rain becomes a picture of God's word accomplishing its purpose, Isaiah 55:10 to 11, and in the Gospel of John Jesus cries, 'Streams of living water will flow from within him,' John 7:37 to 38. In Revelation the river of the water of life flows from the throne, with the tree of life yielding fruit each month, Revelation 22:1 to 2. The type falls short in that the psalm's abundance is for one season and must be renewed each year, while the river of the new creation does not fail.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by atonement. David says that iniquities prevail against him and that God atones for the transgressions of the people. The New Testament tells how this happens. God 'presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood,' Romans 3:25, and Jesus 'Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world,' 1 John 2:2. He is also the merciful and faithful high priest who makes atonement for the sins of the people, Hebrews 2:17. The psalm does not explain how God covers sin, and Christ is the answer. The word of verse 3 is fully understood only when it is read beside the cross.

It leads to Christ by access. The psalm pronounces a blessing on the person whom God chooses and brings near to dwell in His courts, and the New Testament says that Christ is the way in. The temple's curtain kept the people out of the Most Holy Place, and believers now have confidence to enter 'by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19 to 20. Jesus Himself called His body the temple, John 2:19 to 21, so the house of God is now found in Him. Paul says that Gentiles who were far off have been brought near, Ephesians 2:13, which is the fulfilment of the 'all people will come to You' of verse 2. The psalm's 'Blessed' is given in full to those in Christ.

It leads to Christ by authority over the sea. The psalm says that God stilled the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the nations. In the Gospels Jesus gets up in the boat and rebukes the wind and the sea, 'Silence! Be still!' and there was a great calm, Mark 4:39. The disciples, who had prayed the psalms all their lives, ask 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. The psalms had said that God alone rules the raging sea, Psalm 89:9, so the question is the right one, and the Gospel leaves the answer to the reader. On another night He comes to them on the sea, the wind dies down, and they worship Him as the Son of God, Matthew 14:32 to 33.

It leads to Christ by provision. The psalm says that God waters the earth and makes the grain grow, and Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, and promises streams of living water, John 7:37 to 38. The Father who sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, Matthew 5:45, sends His Son in the same spirit of kindness, and the Son's death brings to completion the forgiveness the psalm begins with. The pairing of forgiveness and abundance is found in the one person, who says to those who are weary, 'I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28.

As with all links from the psalms, caution is needed. The psalm is a hymn of Israel and its harvest, and its rain is rain. The links to Christ are those the New Testament draws itself, in atonement, access, authority over the sea and provision. The psalm sets out the pattern of a God who forgives and provides, and in Jesus the two are joined in a single act.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as the one who hears prayer. The second verse names Him by that title, and it is a title with a wide reach, since 'all people will come' to Him. The God of Zion is approachable and is not bound to a people by ethnicity alone. He is the God to whom vows are made and who keeps covenant, and yet He is also the One who listens. Before the psalm says anything of His power, it says that He hears.

He is the God who forgives. The phrase 'You atone for our transgressions' is placed early, and it governs what follows. The confession that iniquities prevail does not alter the psalm's confidence that God is greater. Elsewhere the Psalter says that if the LORD kept track of iniquities no one could stand, but that with Him there is forgiveness so that He may be feared, Psalm 130:3 to 4. The God of Psalm 65 is holy, as the 'holiness of Your temple' shows, and He is gracious. His holiness does not turn away the sinner but makes provision, and the sinner is brought near to share in the goodness of the house.

He is the God of power and of order. He forms mountains, girds Himself with might and stills the seas. The sea in ancient thought was the image of chaos, and the nations in tumult were its human counterpart. The psalm says that both are calmed by the same God without effort or contest. Elsewhere the Bible says that He set boundaries for the sea, Job 38:8 to 11, and that He is majestic above the roar of many waters, Psalm 93:3 to 4. The psalm places this power in the service of His people, so that the same strength that makes the mountains is the strength that answers those who pray.

He is the God who provides, and the psalm draws attention to His care in detail. He attends to the earth, waters it, levels its ridges, softens it with showers and blesses its growth. The language is that of a farmer at work, and God is given the verbs. The psalm does not reduce nature to a machine or to a set of rival powers. It sees the rain as His doing, and it sees the year as a crown that He places. There is a generosity in the picture: the wilderness pastures overflow, and even the hills and valleys are pictured as celebrating.

He is the God of all the earth. Those who live far away fear His wonders, and the dawn and sunset are made to shout for joy. The psalm teaches that His works are visible to the nations and that He is the hope of the farthest seas. This is not an abstract universalism. It is the claim that the God who meets His people at Zion has also been speaking to the world through rain, harvest and the turning of the day, as Paul later says, Acts 14:17.

For worship, the psalm teaches gratitude in two directions. It gives thanks for the forgiveness that no farmer or pilgrim could earn, and thanks for the food that no one could make alone. It invites the worshipper to praise without a trace of anxiety, since the God who atones and waters is a God who does not withhold. It also shows the unity of a believer's life: the prayer of the sanctuary and the work of the field belong to the same worship.

crossReferences.note: 'Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.' It is the same vow language as Psalm 65:1, where vows are fulfilled in Zion. Together they show that praise in Israel involved keeping promises made in distress, so that gratitude was public and had a cost.

A prayer that God would deliver and 'atone for our sins,' for the sake of His name. It uses the same verb as Psalm 65:3 with God as subject and sins as object. The two texts show that Israel knew atonement as something God gives, not something the people produce, even where an offering was part of the practice.

A live coal touches Isaiah's lips and the angel says his iniquity is removed and his sin atoned for. The scene gives a picture of Psalm 65:3 in action: a person overwhelmed by his sin is cleansed by God's own provision, and the cleansing leads straight into service and praise.

God waters the mountains from His chambers and provides crops for man to cultivate. It parallels the second half of Psalm 65, where the rain and the grain are the direct work of God. The fuller creation hymn shows that Psalm 65's picture belongs to a wider vision of a world sustained by God.

Rain and snow come down and water the earth, and God's word does not return empty. The passage joins the image of rain with the pardon offered earlier in the chapter, and it ends with the mountains bursting into song. It resembles Psalm 65 in both its pairing of pardon and rain and its singing hills.

Paul and Barnabas tell a crowd in Lystra that God has not left Himself without testimony, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons and filling hearts with food and gladness. It is the psalm's vision of God's care carried into a Gentile setting, where the harvest is used as evidence of the Creator.

The Father causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. Jesus draws on the same conviction as Psalm 65, that rain is God's gift, and makes it a model for loving enemies. The psalm's 'all people' receive His provision before they know Him.

Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and the disciples are overwhelmed with fear and ask who He is. The scene is an enacted commentary on Psalm 65:7. The power the psalm gives to God over the roaring seas is exercised by Jesus with a word, and the question the disciples ask is the question the psalm teaches the reader to answer.

God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood. It names the way in which God's atonement in Psalm 65:3 is accomplished, and it explains why He could pass over sins in His forbearance. It is the New Testament's answer to the psalm's claim that God covers transgressions.

Those who were far away are brought near through the blood of Christ, and through Him both groups have access to the Father. It is the fulfilment of Psalm 65:2 and 65:4, in which all people come and the one chosen is brought near. It shows that the psalm's blessing was always meant to reach beyond Israel.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the tree of life bears fruit each month. It is the final form of the psalm's 'streams of God' that are full of water, and of the crowned year. The earth's abundance in Psalm 65 is a foretaste of the new creation's unfailing supply.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that begins in the first chapter of the Bible. When God made the world He gathered the waters into seas and let the dry land appear, Genesis 1:9 to 10, and He gave the plants and the grain for food. Adam was put in a garden that was watered and fruitful. Sin brought thorns and toil, and the ground was cursed. The psalm is the voice of a people who live east of the garden and yet still receive rain and harvest, and who know that the gifts of a ruined world are not deserved. Their first word is confession, and then they can see the year as a crown.

It looks back to the covenant with Noah, in which God promised that seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter would never cease, Genesis 8:22. It looks back to the rains promised in the land, Deuteronomy 11:14, and to the prayer of Solomon that God would forgive and send rain, 1 Kings 8:35 to 36. It looks forward in the prophets, where the land is healed after the locusts, Joel 2:23 to 26, and the wilderness rejoices and blossoms, Isaiah 35:1 to 2. The link between pardon and abundance is thus made early and kept.

The story comes to its centre in Christ. The sins that prevailed against the worshipper are covered by the atoning sacrifice, Romans 3:25, and the people are brought near through His blood, Ephesians 2:13. The Lord of the sea and the wind stills the storm in front of His disciples, Mark 4:39, and He feeds the hungry and gives living water. Paul says that the creation itself waits for the children of God to be revealed, since it too was subjected to futility in hope of being set free, Romans 8:19 to 22. The psalm's singing hills are a preview of that liberation.

The new creation is the psalm completed. The one who atones dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3, the sea that symbolised chaos is no more, Revelation 21:1, and the river flows from the throne with trees that bear fruit each month and leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:1 to 2. The nations that in the psalm fear His wonders come into the city. The worship that began with a vow in Zion ends with a world full of praise, and the crown on the year becomes a crown that never needs to be renewed.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say God does for transgressions, in verse 3?

options.text: He atones for our transgressions.
options.note: This confession grounds the psalm's praise in forgiveness before it turns to creation's bounty.

options.text: He ignores them as though they never happened.
options.note: The psalm names active atonement, not simple disregard, as God's work.

options.text: He requires the worshipers to atone for themselves first.
options.note: The verse explicitly credits God, not the worshipers, with making atonement.

options.text: He postpones dealing with them until a future age.
options.note: The verse describes atonement as God's present action, not a postponed one.

quiz.q: What does God do to the seas and the nations, in verse 7?

options.text: He stills the roaring of the seas and the tumult of the nations.
options.note: This links cosmic and political power under God's single sovereign authority.

options.text: He causes them both to rage without limit.
options.note: The verse describes God stilling, not intensifying, the seas and nations.

options.text: He ignores the nations and focuses only on the natural world.
options.note: The verse names both seas and nations together as objects of God's stilling power.

options.text: He divides the seas from the nations permanently.
options.note: The verse does not describe separation; it describes God quieting both alike.

quiz.q: What image describes God's care for the earth, in verses 9-10?

options.text: He attends to the earth, waters it, and softens it with showers to bless its growth.
options.note: This pictures God's personal, attentive care for the physical land and its harvest.

options.text: He leaves the earth's fruitfulness entirely to human effort.
options.note: The verses credit God directly with watering and softening the earth for growth.

options.text: He withholds rain until people prove themselves worthy.
options.note: The verses describe generous, attentive provision, not withheld blessing pending merit.

options.text: He causes the ground to remain dry and barren.
options.note: The verses describe abundant watering and blessing, the opposite of barrenness.

quiz.q: How does creation itself respond to God's bounty, in verses 12-13?

options.text: The pastures overflow, the hills are robed with joy, and the valleys shout and sing.
options.note: The psalm pictures creation itself joining in joyful praise at God's provision.

options.text: The land remains silent and unaffected.
options.note: The psalm explicitly describes creation shouting and singing in response.

options.text: Only the human worshipers respond; creation itself is unmentioned.
options.note: Verses 12-13 specifically describe pastures, hills, and valleys responding, not only people.

options.text: The flocks and grain are destroyed by the abundance of rain.
options.note: The passage describes flourishing abundance, flocks and grain thriving, not destruction.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament connect this psalm's two central themes, atonement and power over creation, to Christ?

options.text: Christ is presented as the atoning sacrifice, and He exercises the same authority over storms that this psalm gives to God alone.
options.note: Romans 3:25 and Mark 4:39 together show Christ fulfilling both the atonement and the cosmic authority this psalm attributes to God.

options.text: The New Testament separates these themes entirely, applying only one to Christ.
options.note: Both themes, atonement and authority over nature, are explicitly applied to Christ in the New Testament.

options.text: Neither theme appears anywhere in the New Testament.
options.note: Both atonement, Romans 3:25, and authority over storms, Mark 4:39, appear directly in the New Testament applied to Christ.

options.text: The New Testament applies both themes only to future events, never to Christ's earthly ministry.
options.note: Mark 4 describes an event during Christ's earthly ministry, and Romans 3:25 describes His accomplished atoning death, both already fulfilled.

questions: The psalm joins forgiveness of sin and the abundance of harvest into a single song of praise. Where in your own life do you tend to separate spiritual gratitude from gratitude for physical, everyday provision, and what would it look like to join them together this week?

Verse 3 confesses, 'when iniquities prevail against me, You atone for our transgressions.' What sin or guilt do you need to bring honestly to God today, trusting His atonement rather than trying to manage it yourself?

God stills the roaring seas and the tumult of nations with the same power, verse 7. What raging circumstance, whether personal or in the wider world, do you need to entrust to God's stilling power today?

The psalm pictures creation itself, hills, pastures, and valleys, shouting and singing at God's bounty, verses 12-13. What ordinary provision in your own life, easily taken for granted, deserves fresh, specific thanks today?

Christ fulfills both this psalm's atonement and its authority over creation. How does holding both truths together, that Christ has both forgiven your sin and rules over your circumstances, change how you pray about a current need?

translationNotes.note: Atone renders kaphar, to cover over or make propitiation, naming forgiveness as God's own active work rather than something the worshiper accomplishes.

You make the dawn and sunset shout for joy can also be rendered where morning dawns and evening fades You call forth songs of joy, either reading picturing all creation, east to west, responding to God with praise.

For You prepare our grain by providing for the earth can also be rendered to provide the people with grain, for so You have ordained it, both readings crediting God directly with the harvest's provision.
